The proposed DrivingDojo dataset is the first dataset designed for training interactive world models with complex driving dynamics. All four reviewers have provided positive feedback, and it is recognized as a valuable contribution worthy of acceptance.

It is recommended that the authors continue to maintain and enhance the dataset by addressing some current limitations, such as the single camera setup and the absence of maps, traffic lights, and trajectories of other agents.

Dear Authors,

Thank you for your detailed response to the review comments. I appreciate your efforts in addressing the concerns, and I look forward to the release of your dataset in the near future. Based on your response, I will raise my score to 6 when I can edit the review.

Thank you for your valuable suggestions. Below are our responses to your comments:

**Q1: Additional annotations of the dataset.**

Thank you for your question. Our dataset is specifically designed to address the data gap in video world modeling tasks. Currently, researchers are limited to using existing perception datasets like nuScenes and Waymo, which are not optimally suited for this purpose. Our dataset aims to provide a more appropriate and specialized resource for video world modeling research. We place greater emphasis on the diversity of video scenes and behaviors, which is a point we aim to highlight in Table 1. Each dataset has its own advantages and focal points, and we will provide additional information on the perceptual strengths of other datasets. Furthermore, the collected data includes information from multiple sensors, along with annotations for agent detection, trajectories and map info. We may consider supplementing this information in the future version when exploring end-to-end planning.

**Q2: Improvement of driving policy.**

Thank you for the constructive suggestion. Our core motivation in this paper is to explore world models for autonomous driving, emphasizing the importance of predicting long-tail events and interactions. We believe that predicting interactive behaviors is central to what a world model should investigate, rather than just focusing on simple action changes in the ego vehicle. Additionally, long-tail objects and complex interactions are crucial for learning end-to-end driving policies. This will be a focus of our future work, where we aim to train on complex scenarios to potentially learn more robust driving policies. We will also consider releasing multi-sensor data in the future to support end-to-end autonomous driving research.

**Q3: Text descriptions and potential usage.**

Thank you for your question. The description provided in meta.json is brief and only represents a specific category, such as sudden braking caused by dynamic objects or unexpectedly appearing pedestrians. In the full version of the dataset, we also utilized VLM models to provide more detailed descriptions, as illustrated in the example below. Although we do not explore applications in this paper, we expect that this information will serve as knowledge that can aid future model generation and understanding, such as training for text-conditioned long-tail case generation. We hope that our dataset will contribute to research in these areas in the future.

long text example:

[videos/140151_s20-437_1685515258.0_1685515278.0/0130_CameraFpgaP0H120.jpg]: 

The image captures an outdoor urban scene with a focus on a traffic intersection. There are multiple vehicles, including sedans and SUVs, indicating a busy thoroughfare. The intersection is marked with yellow lines, and a traffic officer in a white shirt and black trousers is directing traffic with a hand signal. The officer is standing on the pedestrian crossing area, with a traffic cone placed to the side. The background features a row of tall power transmission towers, a cluster of multi-story residential buildings, and a few cars parked along the side of the road. The sky is overcast, suggesting it might be either early morning or late afternoon. The main object in the image is the traffic officer, who is actively engaged in managing the flow of traffic at the intersection.

**Q4: The quality of generated videos and limitations.**

Thank you for your thorough reading and suggestions. The baseline method we used is based on Stable Video Diffusion, which is currently one of the best open-source models available. However, the quality of the generated outputs still leaves something to be desired, particularly regarding the physical realism of lane markings and the generation of long-tail objects, such as rapidly moving small animals or floating balloons. From our experimental experience, we have found that training with high-resolution videos can help alleviate some of these issues. This has also motivated us to further explore more robust video generation models. We agree that these issues are not limitations of the dataset but rather limitations of the baseline method. As noted by **Reviewer eNwo**, we will include the dataset limitations, such as the single-camera setup, in the limitations section.

**Q5: Single camera setting.**

Thank you for your advice, this limitation is also mentioned by **Reviewer eNwo**. We address this issue in the **global response Q1**.

Thank you for your valuable suggestions. Below are our responses to your comments:

**Q1: The open-source availability of the dataset and code.**

We appreciate your concern regarding the open-source availability of our dataset and code. We fully agree that this is of utmost importance. It is, however, common practice to provide a smaller, sample dataset during the review phase, as exemplified by nuPlan and BEHAVIOR-1K. We assure you that we are committed to open-sourcing all data upon acceptance of our work.

We have provided metadata for the whole dataset in https://huggingface.co/datasets/Yuqi1997/DrivingDojo, and in addition, we have include baseline code repo in https://github.com/Robertwyq/Drivingdojo.

**Q2: About 'Multi-agent Interplay' and 'Rich Open-world Knowledge'.**

Thanks for your question. 'Multi-agent Interplay' does not merely refer to many moving objects; instead, it focuses on the interactive behaviors between the ego-car and other road users. For example, this includes scenarios where road users' paths intersect with the ego-car's trajectory and are in close proximity, as well as the investigation of sudden braking situations. The complexity of this exploration is greater than simply considering the number of moving objects. 
Rich Open-world Knowledge' indeed includes many long-tailed scenarios, with data sourced from samples of sudden braking and intervention situations. While existing datasets may contain some of these, they do not specifically focus on exploring them (such as barriers, traffic lights, or roadwork). Additionally, other rare events, like falling objects or uncommon obstructions (e.g., a soccer ball or a herd of sheep), are largely absent. We also provide text labels for these scenarios.

**Q3: Error bars for the experiment.**

Thank you for your suggestion. The results in the table represent averaged values. For FID and FVD metrics, we computed the average over 10 runs. For the AIF metrics, we averaged the results from 5 runs of COLMAP.

| SVD    | nuScenes$\dagger$| OpenDV-2K      | 21.05±0.14   | 395.04±13.68   |
| SVD     | DrivingDojo  | OpenDV-2K      | 19.20±0.16| 343.91±11.83 |

| Generated     | Out-of-Domain  | OpenDV-2K   | 0.175±2.35e-06 | 0.121±5.21e-04 |

**Q4: Benchmark on the ground truth data.**

Thank you for your constructive suggestions. Using GT videos for evaluation is indeed critical information. We have included additional experiments in the table below and will also update this in the revision. It is essential to evaluate more methods; however, there are currently no open-source action-condition models available. In the future, as the community develops, we are willing to assess more methods using our AIF metric.

|**Video Source** |**Action Type** | **Test Dataset** | $\bf{E^{AIF}_x}$ | $\bf{E^{AIF}_y}$ |
|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------
| Ground Truth  |       -        |      -      | 0.036±8.29e-06 | 0.019±7.51e-06 |
| Generated     |   In-Domain    | DrivingDojo | 0.068±8.25e-06 | 0.060±1.12e-04 |
| Generated     | Out-of-Domain  | DrivingDojo | 0.133±6.92e-06 | 0.099±2.57e-04 |
| Generated     | Out-of-Domain  | OpenDV-2K   | 0.175±2.35e-06 | 0.121±5.21e-04 |

**Q5: People's faces in the dataset.**

Thank you for your concerns. Respecting the privacy of other road users is one of the core guideline when building the dataset. We highlighted our mitigation in Section 3.4, "Personal Identification Information (PII) Removal" (Lines 185-188). We employed face and license plate detection algorithms to apply blurring for privacy protection and employed human annotators for checking every video clip to ensure PII removal is correctly performed.

Thank you for your valuable suggestions. Below are our responses to your comments:

**Q1: Performance of tuning SVD on OpenDV-2K.**

Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have added an experiment where we fine-tuned SVD on OpenDV-2K and tested it on the same hold-out OpenDV-2K data. As shown in the table below, from the perspective of FID and FVD metrics, we found that the differences when using DrivingDojo or OpenDV2K for training are minimal, which also suggests the richness of the DrivingDojo scenes. The FID and FVD scores were averaged over 10 runs.
| **Method**                         | **Fine-tuning** | **Evaluation** | **FID** | **FVD**  |
|------------------------------------|-----------------|----------------|---------|----------|
| SVD     | OpenDV-2K               | OpenDV-2K      | 18.27±0.22   | 321.05±5.56   |
| SVD     | -               | OpenDV-2K      | 24.17±0.11   | 580.94±12.40   |
| SVD     | nuScenes$\dagger$| OpenDV-2K      | 21.05±0.14   | 395.04±13.68   |
| SVD     | DrivingDojo   | OpenDV-2K      | 19.20±0.16| 343.91±11.83 |

**Q2: Comprehensive conditions or annotations for the dataset.**

As you pointed out, our dataset includes several tags in the meta.json file related to the video curation process. These tags cover basic attributes such as weather, city, and lighting conditions, as illustrated by the two examples below. Additionally, we provide tags related to events identified during the curation process, such as a red light turning green, a green light turning red, or sudden braking (due to dynamic objects, etc.). This section is described in Appendix Line 580-584.

**Examples:**

{'weather': 'WEATHER_NORMAL', 'location': 'xuzhou', 'time': 'DAY', 'frame_num': 149}

 {'weather': 'WEATHER_RAINY', 'location': 'beijing', 'time': 'DAY', 'frame_num': 169}

**Q3: Generation results besides ego-actions.**

Thank you for your suggestion. The core motivation of our work is to explore action-based generation, as defined by world models, although our method is also applicable to other labels as conditions. We have experimented with text-based conditions, such as weather and short descriptions like "hard braking", and have explored generation under semantic segmentation conditions using results inferred from the InternImage semantic model (mask2former_internimage_h_896_80k_cocostuff2ade20k.pth). Additionally, we have previously tested various conditions on other open-source datasets, including generating results based on LiDAR points and 3D boxes or maps. 

We have uploaded the PDF in the global rebuttal for the visualization. Additionally, you can view visualizations of these results on our project page at https://drivingdojo.github.io, specifically towards the end of the page.

**Q4: Future plans for this dataset.**

Thank you for your suggestion. The dataset released this time has been carefully curated from a database containing 7500 hours of data, comprising high-quality samples. In the future, we aim to explore end-to-end autonomous driving and may consider providing richer sensor information and perception annotations based on this foundation. Currently, semantic segmentation is not part of our plan, but running existing models for semantic segmentation can yield good results, , especially with video segmentation models like SAM2 now being open-sourced. As you mentioned, based on our previous experimental experience, generating videos under semantic segmentation conditions can achieve good results and consistency.

**Q5: About writing issues.**

Thank you for pointing out the writing problem. We will revise this section in future versions to clarify that lane-changing and overtaking are considered lateral behaviors, while acceleration and braking are longitudinal behaviors.

Thank you for your valuable suggestions. Below are our responses to your comments:

**Q1:About single camera setup.**

Thank you for your suggestion. We will highlight in the text that the current version of dataset focuses on single-camera videos and will state this in the limitations section. We opted for a single-camera setup to make the dataset more accessible to a wider audience. Even with just one camera, our dataset already reaches 1.6TB in size. Our current priority is to maximize video diversity. This focus led us to reduce the number of sensors used, allowing us to capture a wider range of scenes. The resulting richness and variety of video content is a key advantage of our dataset compared to previous ones. Our original data collection does include information from multiple cameras and LiDAR data—specifically, it includes three LiDARs: one primary 64-beam LiDAR and two 32-beam LiDARs on the left and right. Additionally, there are four 120-degree cameras positioned at the front, rear, and sides. However, in current version, we have only included data from the front camera, and we plan to enhance these aspects in future versions.

**Q2: Comparison with nuScenes in Table 3.**

Thank you for pointing out this issue. we compared with nuScenes here due to its the de facto benchmark dataset for previous world modeling works. To ensure a fair comparison, we already used 12Hz raw videos instead of 2Hz annotated videos for the nuScenes dataset to increase its data volume. However, in terms of the number of videos (nuScenes' 1k versus DrivingDojo's 18k), there is still a significant difference, and we will clearly indicate this in our experiments. Compared to public datasets like Waymo and nuScenes, which contain only 1k sequences, this also highlights the advantage of our dataset in terms of video quantity and scene diversity. 

**Q3: GPT-4o as a "data curation" strategy.**

Thank you for your question. GPT-4o is utilized in this context to enhance scene descriptions, delving into scene content and generating long-tail cases based on these descriptions. In the curation process, GPT-4o primarily contributes by providing detailed scene descriptions, which are then used to identify open-world scenarios, such as construction sites, puddles, and other similar environments. We used the prompt "I will give a figure with some words you should notice in this scene. Please describe the rare case in autonomous driving in detail."
For example, as mentioned in L568-574 in appendix, the output from GPT-4o is:
"(a) A worker’s helmet rolls on the sidewalk next to the road. (b) A soccer ball is seen flying across the road. (c) A water bucket is depicted falling onto the road. (d) Parcel boxes have fallen onto the road. (e) A dog is crossing the road. (f) A rope is floating over the road. (g) The traffic light turns red. (h) A boom barrier blocks the vehicle from moving forward."

We will provide further clarification on this aspect in the supplementary materials.

summary_and_contributions.value:
This paper introduces a new dataset, called the DrivingDojo dataset, which is targeted towards World Models training for AD systems.
More in detail, the paper introduces 3 different sub datasets:
- DrivingDojo-Action: richer representations for the ego object.
- DrivingDojo-Interplay: Subset of more interesting interactions between vehicles.
- DrivingDojo-Open: Open-world subset, where rare events / objects are in the scene.

The paper also introduces a baseline World Model based on SVD and compares fine-tuning over the new dataset vs. nuScenes (which is also fairly smaller).

review.value: This paper is very well written, and the dataset is a great contribution to the field of E2E AD system, one of the recent hot trends in AD development. Training a World Model is essential for testing E2E AVs and there are not many public datasets in the area that provide longer sensor-rich data with motion annotations.

strengths.value:
* Releases a fairly sized dataset with sensor data useful for world model training
* Attaches important action annotations to the videos
* Reports quite in detail dataset statistics
* The action instruction following metric is quite interesting, basically a displacement error metric but directly from video (important if we are simulating actions that different from the "ground-truth" scenario.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
* The dataset is reasonably sized, but maybe it would be worth highlighting that this is a single camera setup. Other dataset might have more sensor-rich inputs. 

* The comparison with nuScenes on openDV-2K is a bit unfair, as nuScenes has orders of magnitude less data (maybe just point this out?)

limitations.value:
* As mentioned before, I would add something about the single camera setup

The rest of the papers correctly discusses limitations of the dataset and the proposed SVD-based method.

correctness.value: The dataset seems to be constructed in a sound way, and the authors provide extensive information on the data collection in the appendix.

clarity.value: The paper is quite clear and well written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Priori work is correctly mentioned and discussed.

documentation.value: There is enough information about data organization, availability and maintenance.

ethics.value: The authors discuss the PII stripping strategy, an important bit of such a dataset.

additional_feedback.value: One question: in Figure 2 you mention GPT-4o as a "data curation" strategy, but it's not mentioned again in the paper (nor in the appendix). If used, could you please add details about it or otherwise remove it from the figure?

title.value: A new driving dataset for world model learning

summary_and_contributions.value: A new driving dataset containing 150 hours+ driving videos is proposed in this paper for training video generation models for self-driving, aka world model. This dataset features: 1. comprehensive ego-car actions 2. diverse multi-agent interactions 3. rich open-world driving knowledge like crossing animals, falling bottles, and debris, and 4. various weather conditions, which makes this dataset extremely diverse compared to any existing ones. In the experiment, the Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) is finetuned with the proposed dataset. The diverse generation results show the effectiveness of this new dataset.

review.value:
It is good to have a new playground for world-model research. Though some interesting generation results are shown in this paper like the OOD and command-conditioned generation, I believe more possibilities can be unlocked with this diverse data. 

**Question:**
1. In Table. 3, I wonder about the performance of tuning SVD on OpenDV-2K and testing on the same hold-out OpenDV-2K data. If the gap between the fine-tuning results of DrivingDojo and OpenDV-2K is small, it can further suggest that DrivingDojo is diverse enough to partially cover the distribution of OpenDV-2K. Or at least we know to what extent the gap is.
2. The data is curated according to many rules, which would produce comprehensive labels or captions. I wonder if these labels/captions are shipped with the dataset. It could be helpful to condition the model not only on the ego cars' behavior but also the environmental factors, like weather, and rare events like animal-crossing. I want to see some qualitative results where the condition is something besides the ego-car future action.  
3. Are there any future plans for this work? As there are a total of 7500 hours of data and the released part is only 150 hours, would it be possible to have more data released in the future? Also, will more modalities be added in the future like semantics? It is a good pixel-level label that can enhance the generation quality as well.
4. Line 33-35: It seems the "lateral" and "longitude" should be exchanged because lane-changing/overtaking is lateral behavior and acceleration/brake is longitudinal behavior.

strengths.value: As far as I know, this is the first dataset that specifically aims at training world models for autonomous driving featuring diversity. The work is almost complete at this stage and ready to release.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: I would like to see more generation results with other labels besides ego car actions.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces the DrivingDojo dataset, a large-scale driving video dataset designed to advance the development of world models for autonomous driving. The dataset features comprehensive driving maneuvers, multi-agent interplay, and open-world driving knowledge. It aims to enhance the modeling capabilities of world models in simulating real-world driving scenarios. The paper also proposes an Action Instruction Following (AIF) benchmark to evaluate the ability of world models to generate action-controlled future predictions.

review.value:
Pros:
1. The DrivingDojo dataset includes a wide variety of driving maneuvers, multi-agent interactions, rare cases, providing a rich resource for training and evaluating world simulators.
2. The dataset is curated from a large pool of videos from different cities and weather conditions, ensuring a high level of diversity and realism.
3. The metric E_{x}^{AIF} sounds reasonable, providing a good way to measure the performance of world models in following action instructions.
4. The paper provides an insightful limitation analysis, where the examples of hallucination look interesting.

Cons:
1. **I can not find the whole dataset and the code in the paper / supplementary material/ project link.** However, the authors claim that they have included the code and data in the checklist. As this is a benchmark and dataset paper, the open-source availability of the dataset and code is very important.
2. 'Multi-agent Interplay' means the scenarios which have many moving objects and 'Rich Open-world Knowledge' means the long-tailed cases. Is my understanding correct? In my opinion, other existing datasets should also have similar data of these categories.
3. Could you provide the error bars (mean and standard deviation) for your experiments as you claimed in the checklist?
4. As a new benchmark (metric), the authors should evaluate more methods and ground truth videos. Since using COLMAP to estimate trajectories introduces errors, it is necessary to evaluate the ground truth data as well.

summary_and_contributions.value: Motivated by the limited video diversity in current driving datasets, this paper introduces DrivingDojo, the first video dataset of complex driving scenarios. In summary, there are three main contributions based on this new dataset: (1) This dataset consists of three parts, including complete driving actions, diverse multi-agent interplay, and rich open-world driving knowledge. (2) The authors design the action instruction following the task for driving the world model and provide corresponding video world model baseline methods. (3) Benchmark results on both driving video generation and action instruction following show that there are plenty of new opportunities for future driving world model development.

review.value:
**Quality**

The quality of this paper is great. A lot of effort was spent on data collection and curation. The provided dataset contains much more interesting and complex scenarios than existing ones. However, the current format of the dataset seems to be limited to video generation tasks. I think a lot of interesting stuff can be done on it in the future.

**Clarity**

The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

**Originality**

The dataset itself is original. In addition, this paper also proposes an action instruction following (AIF) task for world models, including multiple baselines and metrics.

**Significance**

I think the provided dataset is significant as the current training and evaluation are mostly done in normal and boring scenarios. Broad coverage of complex and long-tail scenarios would benefit the entire autonomous driving community.

strengths.value: I think the provided dataset is significant as the current training and evaluation are mostly done in normal and boring scenarios. Broad coverage of complex and long-tail scenarios would benefit the entire autonomous driving community.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1.	I notice that the provided dataset does not contain information like maps, traffic lights, and trajectories of other agents. This may limit the usage of this dataset only on video generation tasks. Considering Waymo, nuScene, and nuPlan all have that information, the comparison in Table 1 seems not very fair.
2.	This paper only shows the application of training a video world model. However, it seems the long-tail objects and complex interactions are not quite related to this application. It would be more interesting to show the improvement of a driving policy (e.g. an end-to-end model) by training on these complex scenarios.
3.	The text description in the Open-world Knowledge split is short. Longer language descriptions would be helpful for scene understanding. Also, I wonder what the potential usage of it is. I don’t see any application in the paper. 
4.	The quality of the generated video is not good. For example, the double yellow line in Figure 5 is blurred.

limitations.value:
The main limitation, as stated in Section 5.4 by the authors, is the poor consistency of the generated video. I wonder if the quality of generation is even poorer when the scenario contains long-tail objects. However, this seems a limitation of the baseline model on this new dataset. I don’t think it is the main limitation of the dataset.
Besides this point, I think another limitation is that the dataset is only collected with a front-view camera. Considering modern autonomous vehicles have multiple cameras for better FOV, a single camera could be limited in use.

correctness.value: Yes, the dataset is constructed in a sound way.

clarity.value: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The comparison between the new dataset and the existing dataset is summarized in a Table from different perspectives.

documentation.value: Yes, details are included in the appendix. A URL is provided for accessing a small portion of the dataset.

title.value: DrivingDojo Dataset: Advancing Interactive and Knowledge-Enriched Driving World Model

abstract.value: Driving world models have gained increasing attention due to their ability to model complex physical dynamics. However, their superb modeling capability is yet to be fully unleashed due to the limited video diversity in current driving datasets. We introduce DrivingDojo, the first dataset tailor-made for training interactive world models with complex driving dynamics. Our dataset features video clips with a complete set of driving maneuvers, diverse multi-agent interplay, and rich open-world driving knowledge, laying a stepping stone for future world model development. We further define an action instruction following (AIF) benchmark for world models and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed dataset for generating action-controlled future predictions.

                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
